newsitem.title: USA: Seattle-area voters OK $3.9 billion transit plan.
newsitem.headline: Seattle-area voters OK $3.9 billion transit plan.

text.p: A $3.9 billion transit proposal that would ease highway congestion in the Seattle area appeared to be passing easily late on Tuesday.
With 25 percent of the ballots counted, 60 percent of voters in a three-county area favored the proposal and 40 percent opposed it.

It was the second time the Regional Transit Authority had sought voter approval of a plan that included light-rail and improved bus service in parts of the three counties along the chronically congested Interstate 5 corridor.
In March 1995 voters in the transit authority district, a 65-mile-long corridor that stretches from Everett in the north to the southern suburbs of Tacoma, rejected a 16-year, $6.7-billion proposal.

The scaled-back proposal that appeared likely to pass is a 10-year plan to build a 25-mile "starter" light rail system, develop 81 miles of commuter rail lines, and improve bus service and highway express lanes.
Voters were asked to approve a 0.4 percent sales tax and 0.3 percent motor vehicle excise tax to pay for the plan, the same level of taxation they rejected last year.
The Regional Transit Authority estimates that the measure would cost the average household $100 a year in additional taxes.

The tax increases would raise about $1.98 billion over 10 years. Another $1.05 billion would be raised by issuing bonds, and officials anticipate $727 million in federal funding and $155 million in farebox revenues.
